scope: For two commuting finite complex matrices the product of their exponentials, repeated n times, exactly exponentiates n times their sum. Lloyd also treats noncommuting local terms with approximation error.
Two bounded generators in a complete unital real normed algebra obey the Lie–Trotter limit in norm. Trotter’s semigroup theorem also allows generators with domain conditions.
Telescoping bounds the norm difference of nth powers in terms of the one-step difference. For two contractions the factor is at most n.
Bounds the norm of the algebra exponential by exp of the argument norm in the bounded-generator proof.
Finite matrix identities for the controlled SELECT operation and its conjugation by a unitary ancilla preparation. They certify unitarity and one joint matrix element.

In Eqs. (7)–(11), the reference ancilla block of PREPARE† SELECT PREPARE equals the sum of term unitaries weighted by prepared probabilities. Probabilities cₖ/α give H/α, as in the paper’s LCU construction.
The squared weight in the reference ancilla sector is ‖Hψ‖²/α². This is a success probability for a unit system input and is derived from the circuit block.
An orthogonal projector gives an involutory reflection. A product of two symmetric involutions preserves the complex inner product, as required by the signal walk.
The compressed powers of the walk obey a second-order operator recurrence for a symmetric involutory oracle and an orthogonal signal projector.

For the Hermitian involution encoding, compression of the nth walk power gives the Chebyshev polynomial of the signal. A signal eigenvector of value λ acquires the projected amplitude Tₙ(λ), or cos(n arccos λ) for a unit eigenvector. This realizes the signal dynamics of Theorem 2.
A real eigenvalue of the signal on a normalized encoded eigenvector has absolute value at most one.
For a unit encoded eigenvector the state-vector error of a finite weighted sum of projected walks is the scalar approximation error at its eigenvalue.
A degree-two walk polynomial approximates the real-time phase on a unit encoded eigenvector for |t| ≤ 1. Lean gives the explicit error 2|tλ|³/9 for this polynomial.
The first k exponential Taylor terms have norm error at most eˢsᵏ/k! at s = ‖x‖, and converge in a complete normed algebra. These estimates support the segment analysis.
The proof controls the perturbation of repeated powers near a contraction and identifies the norm of the scaled generator −ihH.

For a bounded Hamiltonian the one-segment truncation has a factorial remainder. For self-adjoint H and r positive equal segments the operator error is bounded by (1+δ)ʳ−1, with a corresponding bound on input vectors. Circuit synthesis and query cost require additional results.
Differentiating energy invariance under a linear isometry gives the directional force transformation at a differentiable configuration. The cited work develops a gradient-domain force-field model.
The matrix amplification acting on system blocks equals conjugation and summation with the ancilla-extended Kraus matrices.
The finite Kraus representation gives a complex linear map preserving positivity at every finite ancilla size. This is the representation-to-complete-positivity direction of Choi’s characterization.
Kraus completeness preserves trace with an arbitrary finite ancilla. Combined with complete positivity it preserves normalized positive joint states.
For a finite family of matrices, the completeness relation ΣK†K=I makes the operator sum trace preserving.
The trace of one finite-matrix Lindblad dissipator vanishes by cyclicity. The generator characterization in the paper is a stronger statement.

For one nuclear coordinate on a differentiable potential surface, Newton’s law implies zero instantaneous derivative of kinetic plus potential energy. Existence and accuracy of a molecular adiabatic approximation are additional questions.

When clusters are labeled finite subsets and a weight is the observable minus all proper subcluster weights, Boolean-lattice Möbius inversion recovers that weight. This models the linked-cluster subtraction step.
A cyclic trace identity exchanges propagation of a finite matrix state with propagation of the observable. This is a mathematical prerequisite for the Heisenberg-picture algorithm.
Conjugating an anticommuting string Q by a rotation generated by P with P²=I gives two terms in Q and PQ. The trigonometric rotation follows by choosing its half-angle coefficients.
An exact matrix intertwiner HQ=QK propagates to all powers HᵏQ=QKᵏ.
If QQ† fixes every Krylov vector through degree d, lifting the dth power of Q†HQ reproduces Hᵈv. The paper uses the projected operator for time propagation.
For finite complex trajectory weights of nonzero total weight, sampling with magnitudes and restoring the phase gives the exact reweighted ratio. The average phase has modulus at most one.
For a finite permutation of beads, the sum of harmonic nearest-neighbor spring forces vanishes. This is internal-force cancellation in the ring-polymer model.

For an everywhere-defined bounded self-adjoint Hamiltonian, exp(−itH) is a unitary one-parameter group and is differentiable with the Schrödinger generator. Stone also characterizes general strongly continuous groups via possibly unbounded generators.
The symmetric product VTV has (VTV)†(VTV)=I when each factor does. This verifies norm preservation of a split step and leaves splitting error as a separate estimate.
In a fixed real basis with symmetric linear H, the real and imaginary TD-CI component equations imply zero derivative of their total squared norm.
In a real inner-product space any tangent trial velocity whose residual is orthogonal to the tangent subspace minimizes squared residual over that subspace.
A finite weighted sum of outer products of centered real log-derivative samples has nonnegative quadratic form when the weights are nonnegative. This supplies a sampled variational metric property.
Differentiating the subtractive two-layer ONIOM energy gives full-low force plus model-high force minus model-low force along one coordinate.
For pair-additive dimer energies the two-body fragment expansion equals the sum of monomer energies and pair corrections. Equality assumes the stated pair model.

Restricting the Coulomb constrained search to active densities plus a fixed environment gives an upper bound on the library’s molecular trial-class infimum. Attainment by a compatible split gives equality.
Given error bounds on learned high-minus-low energy corrections at two configurations, the gap error is at most the sum of the endpoint bounds.
For finite supported interaction terms, regional inclusion–exclusion plus terms crossing the two regions reconstructs the union energy. This is an accounting identity for a specified decomposition.
Along a scalar density variation, the derivative of total minus active minus constant frozen energy equals the difference of the first two derivatives.
In an additive density model each active-plus-frozen split must be feasible. Restricting the infimum gives an upper bound, with equality if a split realizes the unrestricted infimum.

Assuming z−D invertible on the eliminated sector, a nonzero eigenvector of a block operator is equivalent to a nonzero solution of the effective equation with unique reconstructed environment component.
For a shared positive rate prefactor, nonnegative inverse temperature β and a barrier error at most ε, the predicted/exact exponential rate ratio lies between exp(−βε) and exp(βε).

At fixed geometry the ONIOM solver error equals the high-level imaginary-time energy excess. A finite gapped model with initial ground overlap gives pointwise convergence and, with an excitation cutoff, an exponential upper bound.
The derivative of a normalized differentiable eigenbranch of a locally symmetric bounded Hamiltonian supplies the high-level force in the one-coordinate ONIOM surface.
On a one-coordinate Newton trajectory driven by the eigenbranch force and both MM forces, kinetic plus layered electronic potential energy has zero derivative.
For a nonempty finite canonical ensemble and β>0, the difference of free energies is −β⁻¹ log of the reference expectation of exp(−βΔU).
For a 1D uniform grid with homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries and mode index 1 through N, the sine mode is nonzero and diagonalizes the second-difference stencil with its explicit eigenvalue.

Given finitely many eigenvectors with nonzero eigenvalues, multiplying their reciprocally weighted superposition by A recovers the input superposition. HHL’s approximation, success probability and complexity need further proofs.
Squared branch norms ‖Kᵢψ‖² are nonnegative and sum to one for a normalized input under Kraus completeness. This extends the probability rule to a finite generalized measurement.
Given orthogonal idempotent branch operators, conditioning on a positive-probability projection yields a unit state with probability one of the same outcome on repetition.

For a normalized qubit and diagonal weak branches of strength η in [−1,1], Lean computes the branch probabilities and posterior z polarization. This is an explicit measurement example in the setting of weak-measurement decomposition.
Finite Fourier orthogonality yields unit readout amplitude on the exact eigenphase grid point and zero at every other grid point. Off-grid phase error is a separate analysis.
For a differentiable eigenbranch in a real Hilbert space and bounded differentiable H, normalization and symmetry at the evaluation point give E′=⟨ψ,H′ψ⟩.

For known distinct real energies, exact samples at n uniformly spaced imaginary times with positive spacing identify n discrete amplitudes by a Vandermonde argument. Silver et al. study ill-conditioned noisy analytic continuation.
A real-coefficient finite Pauli decomposition reconstructs the Hamiltonian expectation as the coefficient-weighted sum of measured term expectations.

For equally many calibrated ±1 shots per term with pairwise independence, Lean proves unbiasedness and bounds the energy-estimator variance by Σcᵢ²/n. The statistics lemma also gives the exact variance.

Computational-basis identities connect the repository’s Pauli expansion to normalized traces against Pauli strings and linear combinations. These support the evaluation in Appendix D, equations (D.7)–(D.8).
Conjugation by a single-site Z multiplies a Pauli word by −1 when the word carries X or Y there and by +1 otherwise. This identifies the sum in equation (D.8).
Equation (D.7). For a Hermitian involutory n-qubit butterfly the squared real coefficients in the concrete Pauli basis sum to one.
Equation (D.8). For a Hermitian involutory evolved butterfly, its normalized first-order OTOC with local Z equals one minus twice the squared Pauli weight of words that anticommute with Z.
Dropping words only from the final sum in (D.8) overestimates the exact OTOC by twice their discarded anticommuting weight. The propagation error of the paper’s window algorithm requires Theorem 1.
The unnormalized trace of (A ⊗ B) times the global swap equals Tr(AB). This contraction identity underlies the two-copy readout.

Equation (III.2). The normalized four-point trace equals the normalized two-copy trace of the evolved butterfly tensored with itself, the doubled probe and the global swap. This is the readout used for window propagation.
Appendix A, Fact 1. Conjugation by U ⊗ U fixes both identity and swap, here for any finite-dimensional unitary U. These invariant tails are used in the window representation.

Theorem 17, Eq. (32). For a finite-dimensional projected unitary encoding and a phase list realizing P, compressing the alternating word gives the odd or even singular-value transform of the encoded matrix. Orthonormal frames represent the two projector ranges. The result includes the empty phase word.

Corollary 8 and Theorem 17, Eq. (32). For a complex polynomial of positive degree d satisfying the paper’s parity and magnitude conditions, d real phases realize P exactly and its alternating unitary word implements the singular-value transform on the specified input and output spaces.

The two cases of Theorem 17, Eq. (32). The compressed alternating unitary word transforms the singular values by the response polynomial of a prescribed odd or even phase list. The even word uses the adjoint oracle and both outer projections onto the input space.

Corollary 8, Eq. (14). The response polynomial of a length-d list of real phases equals a prescribed positive-degree complex polynomial under the parity and magnitude hypotheses. Qatlib also proves minimal length and parity for any realizing list.
